entries.text: Letitia Carson is born, enslaved, in Kentucky — “sometime between 1814 and 1818”. Nothing is known of her early life, or how she came to Missouri before 1845.
entries.source: The Search for Letitia Carson, I, page 4

entries.text: David Carson comes to America from County Antrim with his older brothers and sisters, at about eighteen. The creator writes that he was “most likely” raised Presbyterian.
entries.source: The Search for Letitia Carson, I, page 4

David Carson becomes an American citizen.
entries.source: The Search for Letitia Carson, I, page 6

entries.text: The family settles in a cabin they build on David Carson’s 640-acre Soap Creek Valley provisional land claim.
entries.source: The Search for Letitia Carson, I, page 6

entries.text: Letitia Carson begins the six-month crossing of the Oregon Trail with David Carson.
entries.source: The Search for Letitia Carson, I, page 4

entries.text: Martha Josephine Carson is born near the crossing of the South Platte River.
entries.source: The Search for Letitia Carson, I, page 6

entries.text: Adam Andrew Jackson (“Jack”) Carson is born. Oregon becomes a Territory in the same year.
entries.source: The Search for Letitia Carson, I, page 6

entries.text: The Oregon Donation Land Act reduces the claim to 320 acres, because Letitia was not legally David’s wife — and, the creator adds, could not have held it in any case because she was black.
entries.source: The Search for Letitia Carson, I, page 6

entries.text: Greenberry Smith is appointed administrator and declares that, as slaves, Letitia and the children are property and not entitled as heirs. The creator notes that, this being Oregon, they were not appraised or put up for sale.
entries.source: The Search for Letitia Carson, I, page 6

entries.text: David Carson dies after a short illness.
entries.source: The Search for Letitia Carson, I, page 6

entries.text: Letitia Carson files a Homestead Act claim for 160 acres on South Myrtle Creek, as a widow and single mother of two. Martha is eighteen and pregnant; Jack is almost fourteen. Although the Act includes freed slaves, she does not identify herself as one.
entries.source: The Search for Letitia Carson, I, page 8

Letitia Carson’s homestead claim is certified. She is among the first seventy-one people in the United States so recognised, and the only black woman in Oregon known to have completed such a claim.

The two Lavadour–Carson families move to the Umatilla Reservation to take up Dawes Act allotments. Jack stays with his mother, and she deeds her land to him.

entries.text: Letitia Carson dies and is buried in the Stephens family graveyard, a few miles from her homestead.

disputes.about: When Letitia Carson passed the homestead to her son

positions.says: A warranty deed and a record of sale, both dated 21 July 1884, stand in the Douglas County group.
The creator writes that Letitia deeded her land to Jack in 1887, when the Lavadour families left for the reservation, and his own chapter heading reads “Jack is Given the Land, 1887”.

disputes.note: Both are kept. The Library has not seen a document dated 1887, and does not know whether the creator is describing a second conveyance, a later recording, or a slip.
